'''Lee Cecil Fletcher Sallows''' (born April 30, 1944) is a British electronics engineer known for his contributions to [[recreational mathematics]].  He is particularly noted as the inventor of [[golygon]]s, [[self-enumerating sentence]]s, and [[geomagic square]]s.

==Recreational mathematics==
Sallows is an expert on the theory of [[magic squares]]<ref>[http://www.magic-squares.net/square-update.htm Magic Square Update-2009], September 6, 2009</ref> and has invented several variations on them, including [[alphamagic square]]s<ref>[http://www.daviddarling.info/encyclopedia/A/alphamagic_square.html alphamagic square] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171010024434/http://www.daviddarling.info/encyclopedia/A/alphamagic_square.html |date=2017-10-10 }}, Encyclopedia of Science</ref><ref>[http://digitalcommons.butler.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1149&context=wordways&sei-redir=1#search=%22Lee%20Sallows%20British%22 excerpt from ''Word Play'' by Martin Gardner]</ref> and [[geomagic square]]s.<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/science/2011/apr/03/magic-squares-geomagic-lee-sallows ''Magic squares are given a whole new dimension''], [[The Observer]], April 3, 2011</ref> The latter invention caught the attention of mathematician [[Peter Cameron (mathematician)|Peter Cameron]], who has said that he believes that "an even deeper structure may lie hidden beyond geomagic squares".<ref>[https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn20017#.UfgkFWTXhXc ''Ancient puzzle gets new lease of 'geomagical' life''], [[New Scientist]], January 24, 2011</ref>

In "The lost theorem" published in 1997 he showed that every 3 × 3 magic square is associated with a unique parallelogram on the [[complex plane]], a discovery that had escaped all previous researchers from ancient times down to the present day.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2FBF03024415#page-1 | doi=10.1007/BF03024415 | title=The lost theorem | date=1997 | last1=Sallows | first1=Lee | journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer | volume=19 | issue=4 | pages=51–54 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>  

A [[golygon]] is a [[polygon]] containing only [[right angle]]s, such that adjacent sides exhibit consecutive [[integer]] lengths. Golygons were invented and named by Sallows<ref name="isogons">{{Cite journal |last1=Sallows |first1=Lee |last2=Gardner |first2=Martin |author-link2=Martin Gardner |last3=Guy |first3=Richard K. |author-link3=Richard K. Guy |last4=Knuth |first4=Donald |author-link4=Donald Knuth |date=1991 |title=Serial Isogons of 90 Degrees |url=https://www.jstor.org/pss/2690648 |journal=Mathematics Magazine |volume=64 |issue=5 |pages=315–324 |doi=10.2307/2690648 |jstor=2690648|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and introduced by [[A.K. Dewdney]] in the ''Computer Recreations'' column of the July 1990 issue of ''[[Scientific American]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://geocities.com/hjsmithh/Golygons/GolyWhat.html |title=What is a Golygon? |accessdate=2010-10-08 |url-status=bot: unknown |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20091027155427/http://geocities.com/hjsmithh/Golygons/GolyWhat.html |archivedate=October 27, 2009 }}</ref>

In 2012 Sallows invented and named [[self-tiling tile set]]s—a new generalization of [[rep-tiles]].<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.jstor.org/discover/10.4169/math.mag.85.5.323?uid=3739776&uid=2&uid=4&uid=3739256&sid=21102332189497 | jstor=10.4169/math.mag.85.5.323 | doi=10.4169/math.mag.85.5.323 | title=On Self-Tiling Tile Sets | date=2012 | last1=Sallows | first1=Lee | journal=Mathematics Magazine | volume=85 | issue=5 | pages=323–333 }}</ref>
{{clear}}

==Triangle theorem==
[[File:sallows_triangle_theorem.svg|thumb|left|Visual proof of Lee Sallows's triangle theorem]]
In 2014, Sallows discovered a previously unnoticed result, a way of using the [[Median (geometry)|medians]] to divide any triangle into three smaller triangles, all congruent with one another. Repeating the process on each triangle yields triangles [[Similarity_(geometry)|similar]] to the original but a ninth the area.<ref>Sallows, Lee, "[https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.4169/math.mag.87.5.381 A Triangle Theorem]" ''[[Mathematics Magazine]]'', Vol. 87, No. 5 (December 2014), p. 381</ref>

==Personal life==
Lee Sallows is the only son of Florence Eliza Fletcher and Leonard Gandy Sallows. He was born on 30 April 1944 at [[Brocket Hall]] in [[Hertfordshire]], England, and grew up in the district of [[Upper Clapton]] in northeast London. Sallows attended [[Dame Alice Owen's School]], then located at [[London Borough of Islington|The Angel, Islington]], but failed to settle in and was without diplomas when he left at age 17. Knowledge gained via interest in [[short-wave radio]] enabled him to find work as a technician within the electronics industry. In 1970, he moved to [[Nijmegen]] in the Netherlands, where, until 2009, he worked as an electronic engineer at [[Radboud University]]. In 1975, Sallows met his partner Evert Lamfers, a Dutch [[cardiologist]],<ref>[https://www.cwz.nl/over-cwz/nieuws-en-pers/nieuwsoverzicht/afscheid-van-cardioloog-evert-lamfers-ik-rolde-van-het-ene-in-het-andere/ Farewell to cardiologist Evert Lamfers]</ref> with whom he has lived ever since.
